A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Distribution Transformers work. All pages, including Appendices A–G, are readable, and the text, equations, tables, and rendered figures support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 report original analytical-verification, Gaussian-process, quantum-simulation, and sequential sensor-fusion results, supported by Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–6.

after.justification: Retains original empirical results and reports expanded baseline comparisons and a five-dimensional Gaussian-process evaluation in Sections 4.1–4.3.

M1.justification: The prior and observation embeddings, permutation-equivariant decoder, GMM unembedding, combined loss, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix B's added LayerNorm statement documents an implementation detail without establishing an architectural change.

E1.justification: The GP study expands to a five-dimensional input benchmark in Section 4.2.1 and Appendix E, while retaining the one-dimensional illustration in Figure 4. The analytical, quantum-system, and sequential sensor-fusion task coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: ACE and TabPFNv2 are added to the analytical comparison in Table 1, GP comparison in Table 2, and quantum comparison in Figure 5. Table 2 also adds an evaluated MCMC comparator. Existing VI/SVI, PFN, and sequential EKF/PF comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix E changes the GP lengthscale meta-priors from uniform [1,2] for both parameters to [100,105] for concentration and [100,700] for rate, and changes the input-coordinate range from [0,10] to [0,5]. Added configurations include a 5,000-bucket PFN, TabPFNv2 conditioned on 10,000 samples, and ACE with matched GMM heads and a fixed inference target. These are reported setting changes and added protocols; they do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Figure 3 and Table 1 add a PFN output-resolution comparison using 15 versus 5,000 histogram buckets, testing whether greater histogram capacity improves posterior approximation. Existing narrow/wide meta-prior comparisons, DT component-count comparisons, and sequential case study remain.

E5.justification: Both versions already report 95% confidence intervals for analytical KL divergence and uncertainty values or bands elsewhere. The additional results follow the existing reporting practice; no new seed information, repeated-run protocol, confidence-interval procedure, or significance test is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 5 add comparator results and revise existing values. For example, analytical SVI narrow-prior KL changes from 0.0423 to 0.0425. Table 2 replaces DT PPD/hyperposterior NLL values of -0.32/0.81 with 0.81/0.31 under changed GP conditions, so these are not same-setting gains. The GP speed ranking also changes: v1 favors DT, whereas v2 reports PFN at 9.2 seconds versus DT at 9.5 seconds. Table 3's sequential results are unchanged.

T1.justification: The GMM and DT definitions, Proposition 3.1, and its loss-to-KL derivation in Appendix A retain the same mathematical substance. The new conjugacy discussion introduces no additional formal result or proof.

C1.justification: V1 claims that prior adaptation without retraining is 'never before accomplished'; v2 redefines the central contribution around the combination of prior flexibility, approximate conjugacy, and sequential composition. The conclusion also replaces 'near-exact' inference with competitive expected-NLL performance. The abstract's broad speed and flexibility claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 speculates that DT's advantage over ACE comes from attention over mixture components and attributes MCMC's GP shortfall to instability and non-convergence. These are added interpretations, without corresponding new mechanism ablations. The accompanying claim that ACE is second-best overgeneralizes Table 1: the narrow-prior PFN-5000 KL of 0.0038 is below ACE-5's 0.0094.

D1.justification: V2 adds an anonymized code link, ACE implementation and training details, and TabPFNv2 conditioning instructions in Appendix B and Table 4. It explicitly documents LayerNorm and revises quantum-study training times, including DT from 432 to 222 seconds, while retaining the stated hardware and existing DT training budgets.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 substantially replaces the classical approximate-inference survey with positioning around amortized inference, neural processes, simulation-based inference, and sequential composition. It adds discussion of ACE, TabPFN developments, BayesFlow, sensitivity-aware inference, and prior-amortized posterior estimation, acknowledging prior-flexible approaches absent from v1's positioning.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list, and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten around prior amortization and conjugacy. V2 also revises the conclusion, adds a checklist and Supplementary Materials heading, removes the generic Impact Statement, and updates affiliation text. Much of the method exposition remains intact.

P2.justification: V2 changes typography, title and author layout, running headers, and float placement throughout. Figures 3 and 5 are replotted with expanded legends and changed axes, and Tables 1, 2, and 4 gain comparator rows. Figures 1, 2, 4, 6, and 7 retain their substantive displays despite layout changes.

improvement.justification: The added ACE, TabPFNv2, and MCMC comparisons make the empirical assessment more informative, while revised positioning acknowledges other prior-flexible methods and better qualifies the contribution. Added implementation and code-access information also helps. These gains are limited by text–table inconsistencies: Section 4.2.1 still calls DT fastest despite Table 2 favoring PFN, and Section 4.1 overstates ACE's ranking and GMM superiority in the narrow-prior comparison.
